accept: Knapping a flint flake and lashing it to a split wooden shaft with sinew gives a hafted point that can be thrown.
Wet clay is pressed into a mould and fired in a pit, which drives off water and sinters the body into a hard pot.
Twisting plant fibres into a cord under tension locks the strands by friction so the rope holds a load.
Heating copper ore with charcoal in a closed furnace reduces the oxide to metal that pools at the bottom.
Grinding grain between two stones breaks the husk and crushes the kernel into coarse flour.
Soaking hide in tannin-rich bark liquor cross-links the collagen, so the leather stops rotting and stays supple.
Drilling a hole through a bone with a pointed flint and polishing the edge produces a needle that can draw thread.
Hammering heated bronze on an anvil flattens and work-hardens the edge, giving a sharper blade.
Packing damp clay around a reed frame and drying it in the sun creates a rigid brick wall panel.
Mixing lime with sand and water, then letting it cure, produces a mortar that binds stones into a wall.
Stretching a sinew string between the ends of a bent wooden stave stores elastic energy that launches an arrow.
Fire-hardening the tip of a sharpened wooden stick removes moisture and makes the point stiffer for thrusting.
Spinning wool on a weighted spindle draws and twists the fibres into a continuous yarn for weaving.
Melting sand with soda ash at high furnace heat fuses the grains into glass that can be blown into a vessel.
Fixing a wheel to a rotating axle under a wooden platform lets a load roll with far less drag than sliding.
Pouring molten metal into a stone mould lets it cool into a casting with the shape of the cavity.
Boiling seawater in a shallow clay pan evaporates the water and leaves salt crystals behind.
Sewing hide strips with bone needles and sinew thread joins them into a garment panel.
Smoking meat over a slow fire dries the surface and deposits preserving compounds that slow spoilage.
Binding straw into bundles and tying them to rafters forms an overlapping layer that sheds rain.
Rubbing a hardwood spindle against a notched board generates friction heat until tinder glows and catches.
Carving a log with an adze and charring the hollow with embers excavates a hull that floats and carries a person.
Heating iron bloom and folding it under the hammer expels slag and consolidates the metal into a usable bar.
Quenching a hot steel blade in water traps carbon in a hard structure at the edge.
Pressing olives under a weighted beam squeezes the oil out of the crushed flesh into a collecting channel.
Rolling out wet papyrus strips in crossing layers and pressing them while drying bonds the fibres into a writing sheet.
Setting a lens of polished crystal in a tube focuses light, so a distant object appears larger.
Attaching a long counterweighted arm to a sling uses leverage to throw a stone much farther than by hand.
Fitting a gear train to a water wheel transfers the river's rotation to a millstone at a useful speed.
Stretching dried gut over a hollow gourd body gives a string whose length sets the pitch when plucked.
Weaving willow rods around upright stakes forms a basket wall rigid enough to carry grain.
Burning limestone in a kiln releases carbon dioxide and leaves quicklime, which slakes with water into plaster.
Beating a copper sheet over a stake raises it into a bowl shape as the metal stretches under repeated blows.
Cutting a thread into a rod and cutting a mating thread inside a nut lets rotation turn into a strong clamping force.
Winding insulated wire around an iron core carries current, which magnetises the core while the circuit is closed.
Passing steam through a cylinder with a piston converts heat expansion into a back-and-forth push on a rod.
Etching lines into a wax-coated copper plate with acid bites the exposed metal so ink can be held in the grooves.
Melting tallow around a braided wick lets the wick draw fuel upward by capillary action and burn steadily.
Dyeing yarn in a mordant bath of alum fixes the colour into the fibre so it resists washing.
Drying a thin slice of fruit on a flat stone in sun and wind removes water so it keeps for months.
Fitting a hollow reed with finger holes lets the player vary the vibrating air column length to change pitch.
Casting a lead weight on a cord gives a plumb line whose steady vertical direction can check a wall.
Stacking dressed stones in staggered courses spreads load so the wall carries weight without a binder.
Shaping a flat stone with a shallow hollow and rubbing a round stone over seeds crushes them into paste.
Boiling animal bones and hide scraps extracts collagen that forms a sticky glue as it cools.
Heating a clay-coated charge with a bellows raises furnace temperature enough to melt a bronze alloy.
Tying feathers to the shaft end of an arrow stabilises its flight by increasing drag at the rear.
Setting two flat grinding wheels on a shaft with a hand crank lets the operator sharpen a blade quickly.
Fixing a pivoting beam above a well with a bucket and counterweight lowers the effort needed to lift water.
Knotting a long fibre net with a regular mesh lets water pass while a catch of fish stays inside.
